content.title: Reply to Reviewer mFcP
content.comment: Thanks for your insightful reviews. For your question about aggregation, it is just a simple operation to collect all synthetic examples from different clients in the dimension of the batch. Specifically, suppose the synthetic dataset $S_k$ of the client k has the shape $(n_k^S, h, w, c)$ ($h, w, c$ denote height, width, and channel of the image respectively), and then aggregation concatenates $S_k$ in the first dimension to form a larger dataset $(\sum_k{n_k^S}, h, w, c)$. We will make the technical details more clear and distinguish our paper from prior works.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer nvFf
content.comment: We appreciate that you pointed out the potential problem of our privacy analysis with respect to the synthetic dataset’s initialization. We have revised the algorithm of FedDM to adopt randomized initialization when comparing differential privacy with other baseline methods and results show that FedDM still outperforms model averaging based methods significantly under the same privacy budget. We will include this comparison in the modified version. In addition, we will also take your constructive suggestions into account to add more experiments and make the analysis more clear and rigorous in the latest version.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer aK1y
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable comments. However, the DP guarantee of FedDM still holds even though the synthetic dataset instead of its gradient is transmitted to the server. It is due to the robustness to post-processing [1], an important property of differential privacy which we forgot to include in the main paper by mistake. In particular, this property ensures the results of differentially private computations can be safely released because any post-processing computation will also be differentially private. Back to our setting, leveraging the synthetic dataset to update the network at the server’s side is a type of post-processing operation, and thus DP guarantee is maintained as long as the generation of synthetic dataset is trained with DP. This property has also been deployed in similar applications such as [2], where the synthetic text generated from a DP-trained language model was used in various downstream tasks and still preserved privacy. We will introduce the post-processing property in our revised version and make the analysis more rigorous.

[1] Dwork, C., & Roth, A. (2014). The algorithmic foundations of differential privacy. Foundations and Trends® in Theoretical Computer Science, 9(3–4), 211-407.

[2] Yue, X., Inan, H. A., Li, X., Kumar, G., McAnallen, J., Sun, H., ... & Sim, R. (2022). Synthetic Text Generation with Differential Privacy: A Simple and Practical Recipe. arXiv preprint arXiv:2210.14348.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes to communicate local synthetic data instead of local models in federated learning. The motivation is that communicating surrogates to local loss functions allows the server to find a more suitable global model than simple averaging of local models. The synthetic data is created to minimize the difference in network output and last layer representation around for all network parameters close to the current model. The server aggregates all local synthetic data, trains the global model and distributes it to the clients for another round of synthetic data generation. Using suitable noise on synthetic data before communication ensures differential privacy.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- novel approach to federated learning
- large gain in accuracy over most state-of-the-art FL methods

Weaknesses:
- the proof of differential privacy is not convincing
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is written clearly, the approach is novel, and the experiments are reproducible, since the source code is provided.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The proposed approach is interesting and relevant to the community. It is particularly interesting that the synthetic dataset with differential privacy suffices to capture enough properties of local data to improve global train that much. Without privacy, this was a trivial result - basically amounting to centralizing local data. Given that the paper proves differential privacy for the synthetic data, the approach becomes non-trivial. 

My concern is that the proof of differential privacy might not be correct. It hinges on the fact that the gradient of Eq. 9 can be regarded as the gradient of the loss wrt. the original samples. From DP-SGD it is known that sharing gradients using the Gaussian mechanism preserves privacy, since the gradient is the only information communicated, so as long at it is differentially private, all further results (including the trained model) will be differentially private. Now this paper argues that given the equivalence of the gradient of Eq. 9 and the modified gradient wrt. the original data, the shared information is similar in FedDM and DP-SGD and thus differential privacy holds for both. This, however, would only be true if FedDM only shares the gradients of Eq. 9. It does, however, share the synthetic dataset. I do not see how the privacy of the gradients guarantees the privacy of the synthetic dataset. 

If I was wrong and the privacy analysis holds, it seems to imply that the Gaussian mechanism could even be applied to the original data, since $\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{D}$ is a solution to Eq. 9. This would contradict results on private data sharing.

If the authors could expand on their proof and indeed show that differential privacy holds, this paper would be a great contribution. In its current form, though, the paper did not convincingly show that differential privacy does hold.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a federated learning framework where each client sends the server a small number of synthetic examples that approximate the objective locally. The server then uses these synthetic examples to update the global model. The paper shows how this can be done with instance-level differential privacy and presents convincing numerical results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

- (S1) The idea of generating locally valid synthetic data is novel in federated learning. 
- (S2) The experimental results demonstrate a strong savings in terms of communication (although other issues exist - see below). 
- (S3) Privacy of the proposed approach is a strong positive (although issues exist with rigor -- details below). 

**Weaknesses**:

- (W1) I think there might a flaw in the privacy argument (correct me if I am mistaken and I'll update my score). The initialization of the of the synthetic data to real samples (as mentioned in section 4.1, paragraph "Hyperparameters") can leak privacy. This does not show up in the usual DP-SGD analysis because the initialization is assumed to be unrelated to the data (random init), but shows up in the setting of this paper.
- (W2) The privacy analysis is sloppy and not rigorous. For instance, the distinction between instance-level and client-level DP is not made clear ($D_1, D_2$ are not defined in Eq. (12)). The analysis should appear as a formal mathematical statement in full rigor.  
The total privacy loss of each algorithm depends on the number of local updates, the number of parameters (via the clipping norm). It is also common practice to treat the clipping norm as a hyperparameter and report results with the best one. 
- (W3) Experiments: the number of local epochs is typically treated as a hyperparameter as well, and is typically taken to be small (see e.g., https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.06917). It is possible that the number of local epochs chosen in Section 4 is too large and this hurts the baselines. 
- (W4) Connection to Renyi MMD is tenuous. Match losses (Eq. 7) is much easier than matching distributions (Eq. 8/9).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity** 

- (C1) The paper seems to build heavily on Zhao et al. 2020, Zhao & Bilen 2021a. It would help to recall the key results from these papers (in its present draft, the paper basically requires that the reviewers be familiar with these papers as well). 
- (C2) I though $f_k$ and $\hat f_{r, k}$ were scalars. Then, why does Eq. (7) use a norm $\| \cdot \|$? Besides, wouldn't we want to match gradients and not losses?
- (C3) Details are missing in Algorithm 1. How are $S_k$ initialized? (I know this is explained in Section 4, but this information needs to be specified here). Is $S_k$ maintained as state between updates?
- (C4) Some symbols are not explained. For example: $\mathcal{H}$ in eq. (8)
- (C5) It would more transparent to describe the loss (9) in terms of losses


**Quality**:

- (Q1) Experiments: the optimization does not seem to have converged within 20 rounds (Figures 2 and 4). To correctly interpret the results of Table 2, it would be good to see the final accuracies after convergence.


**Minor comments**:

- It is more interpretable to talk about the privacy guarantees of DP-SGD using Renyi DP, see e.g. https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.00087
content.summary_of_the_review: Interesting method with strong empirical results. But the privacy analysis is too hand-wavy and might also have some potential flaws (correct me if I'm wrong).

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper is about communication-efficient federated learning. In this work, the authors proposed to construct synthetic sets of data on each client to locally match the distribution of private data through distribution matching. The synthetic data is uploaded to the server for global model training. To protect data privacy, the authors introduced differential privacy into the synthetic data generation process. Extensive experiments are conducted in this work to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed solution.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

-- The authors introduced differential privacy into the synthetic data generation, keeping a good balance between data privacy and final performance.

-- The authors conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed solution. And the authors provide a theoretical analysis of the differential privacy part in their method.

Weakness:

-- The synthetic data generation in this work seems a direct application of Zhao and Bilen, 2021a. It seems that the authors did not condcut technical modification on synthetic data generation itself.

-- To keep the data private, the authors introduced differential privacy in their work, i.e., Line 17/18 in Algorithm 1. It seems a direct application of differental privacy here. 

-- I am a little confused about some technical details in this work. For example, in Eq. 10, it is defined as an aggregation of all synthesized data. What is the dimension of the aggregated result? Is the cadinality of the aggregated result different from the cardinality of the synthesized data before aggregation? Is the aggregation here a combination or a summation along a specific channel?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This work is organized well. However, some techincal details and the novelty need to be clarified.
content.summary_of_the_review: Generally, the authors propose an interesting solution for communication-efficient federated learning in this work. The draft is organized-wll and the movitivation is clear. I am concerned about the technical details and novelty compared to prior works.

content.title: FedDM: Iterative Distribution Matching for Communication-Efficient Federated Learning
content.abstract: Federated learning (FL) has recently attracted increasing attention from academia and industry, with the ultimate goal of achieving collaborative training under privacy and communication constraints. Existing iterative model averaging based FL algorithms require a large number of communication rounds to obtain a well-performed model due to extremely unbalanced and non-i.i.d data partitioning among different clients. Thus, we propose FedDM to build the global training objective from multiple local surrogate functions, which enables the server to gain a more global view of the loss landscape. In detail, we construct synthetic sets of data on each client to locally match the loss landscape from original data through distribution matching. FedDM reduces communication rounds and improves model quality by transmitting more informative and smaller synthesized data compared with unwieldy model weights. We conduct extensive experiments on three image classification datasets, and results show that our method can outperform other FL counterparts in terms of efficiency and model performance. Moreover, we demonstrate that FedDM can be adapted to preserve differential privacy with Gaussian mechanism and train a better model under the same privacy budget.
